sections.title: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

questions.q: Why are the first three years called the foundation years?
questions.answer: Because incredible growth takes place in all domains of development during these years.

questions.q: How do children form relationships?
questions.answer: Through the consistent and continuous presence of caregivers who talk, feed, play and give love and care.

questions.q: Name the primary needs of children mentioned in the passage.
questions.answer: Regular response to feeding, bodily needs and tactile comfort.

questions.q: How do warm responses help the baby's brain?
questions.answer: They form new neural connections in the brain.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Reducing stress means responding to children on ________.
questions.answer: demand

questions.q: Name two things from which caregivers should protect young children.
questions.answer: Any two: loud noise, disturbing visuals, harsh and fast movements, being left alone or ignored.

sections.passage: The first three years are often called the foundation years as incredible growth takes place in all domains of development. Children form relationships through the consistent and continuous presence of caregivers who talk, feed, play and give love and care. Regular response to feeding, bodily needs and tactile comfort are the primary needs of children. Caregivers promote healthy brain development by giving warmth, making eye contact and responding with a pleasant gesture or a hug every time the baby babbles or cries; this forms new neural connections in the brain. Reducing stress means responding to children on demand and protecting them from loud noise, disturbing visuals and harsh, fast movements. Leaving children alone or ignoring them can obstruct their growth and development.

sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (match the columns, true/false, fill in the blanks or one-word answers).

questions.q: Answer in one word or phrase: (i) What does a high-quality ECCE programme provide? (ii) What are the two main types of childcare settings?
questions.answer: (i) A safe and nurturing environment that promotes physical, social, emotional and intellectual development. (ii) Familial (home-based) and non-familial (centre-based) care.
questions.note: April 2024 also asked who should keep close communication (parents and teachers) and what environment they should create (a nurturing one).

questions.q: Answer briefly: (i) What are the benefits of breastfeeding for babies? (ii) Why is it important for caregivers to ensure comfortable clothing for children?
questions.answer: (i) Breast milk is a complete food that protects from infection, builds immunity, reduces illness and death, and gives comfort. (ii) A baby's skin is soft and delicate; soft, loose, clean clothes protect it from stiff materials and discomfort.

questions.q: Answer in one sentence: (i) Mention a step you will take to ensure care and protection of children in an ECCE centre. (ii) What would you conclude if you found an ECCE worker not supervising children during play?
questions.answer: (i) For example: keep the centre physically safe (no sharp objects, covered water, safe play equipment) and supervise children at all times. (ii) The children's safety is at risk; the worker is neglecting a basic duty and needs guidance from the centre head.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (i) Till six months of age, babies get enough nutrition from ________. (ii) Weaning foods are ________ preparations given to babies in the move from mother's milk.
questions.answer: (i) breast milk (ii) semi-solid

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (i) Routines give children a sense of ________ and control over their environment. (ii) Cognitive stimulation is dependent on early attachment and ________ relationships.
questions.answer: (i) security (ii) positive

questions.q: Match: (a) Touch (b) Cleaning the eyes — (i) Hygiene (ii) Comforting and soothing (iii) Immunisation
State True or False: (i) Children are not affected by their external environment. (ii) Anxiety and stress can affect later learning among children.
questions.answer: (i) False. (ii) True.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Mention any four conditions that generally foster a safe, nurturing and stimulating environment for children.
questions.answer: Any four: low child-caregiver ratio; small group size; motivated and sensitive caregivers; positive caregiver-child interaction; age- and developmentally appropriate activities and materials; good health, hygiene and safety practices; trained staff with professional development.

questions.q: What care and protection should an ECCE worker take for children in the centre?
questions.answer: Keep the centre physically safe and supervise children all the time; ensure hygiene, clean water and safe food; follow immunisation and health check-ups; respond warmly to children's needs and protect them from stress, rough handling and neglect so they feel emotionally secure.

questions.q: Why are routines important in caregiving?
questions.answer: Routines give children security and control over their environment and prepare them emotionally for coming changes. Familiar schedules and objects bring continuity and soothe them in times of change; babies learn time, sequence and permanence through the rhythms of care.

questions.q: Why is interest important in a child's learning?
questions.answer: Interest is a form of energy that leads to curiosity and motivates and guides children's engagement with the world. Without interest there is no curiosity, no exploration and no real learning; enthusiastic adult response keeps it alive.
questions.note: Part of a 4-mark question in October 2022.

questions.q: What is kinaesthetic stimulation? Give two activities.
questions.answer: Kinaesthetic means the sense of movement — exploring physical space by moving the body. Activities: lifting the baby up and down in different positions; rocking and swaying to a rhythm; letting the baby crawl over, under and through objects; clapping and snapping while talking.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Explain the significance of sensory stimulation for development.
questions.answer: Infants learn about the world through their senses. Stimulation through sight, sound, smell, taste and touch creates neural pathways in the brain that support later learning, and develops motor skills and the ability to solve simple problems. Visual stimulation (faces, colours, peek-a-boo) builds observation; auditory input (talking, music, natural sounds) builds the base of language; touch (holding, rocking, textures) builds trust and fine motor skills; movement builds balance. Activities should be many and repeated.
questions.note: October 2022 also asked about kinaesthetic stimulation.

questions.q: What role can teachers and parents play in relieving stress among children?
questions.answer: Young children cannot say what troubles them, so they show it by irritability or crying. Parents and teachers should respond sensitively to unusual behaviour, keep routines and familiar objects, give warm physical comfort, listen when children talk about school ('Teacher does not smile'), share information daily so home and centre feel like extensions of each other, and work as a team rather than against each other.

questions.q: What are the different kinds of caregiving systems?
questions.answer: Familial care: by parents or relatives (aunts, uncles, grandparents) at home. Non-familial care: by non-relatives such as babysitters, neighbours or friends in the child's or the provider's home. Organised childcare: crèches, day-care centres, preschools, nursery schools, kindergartens and pre-primary schools, and workplace crèches. Care is also classed as home-based (few children in the provider's home) or centre-based (larger groups in a non-home setting).

questions.q: Describe the principles of caregiving of children under three years.
questions.answer: Supportive and responsive environment: regular response to feeding, bodily needs and tactile comfort gives a secure base and helps children regulate emotions. Responsive relationships and strong life skills: warmth, eye contact, gestures and hugs build neural connections; routines and creative play build independence, curiosity and coping. Reduce sources of stress: respond on demand with multi-sensory interaction and protect children from loud noise, disturbing sights and harsh movements; never leave them alone or ignore them.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: How can parents and teachers work together to support children's development?
questions.answer: Parents, teachers and children are a dynamic triad. Together they must create a nurturing, healthy and safe environment, pass on cultural values and help children master developmental tasks. Children need unconditional love, safe surroundings, supportive teachers, play with peers, self-confidence and guidance. Collaboration: centres keep regular contact; parent workshops share childcare practices and ways of discipline; daily exchanges at drop-off and pick-up track milestones and spot delays early. Channels: appointments for special issues, daily conversations, sharing home routines, email, messages and phone. Children's views: parents should listen when children talk about school; sensitive responses from both relieve stress. They must work as a team, not in opposition.
questions.note: April 2022 asked: how do parents and teachers contribute to the overall development of children?

questions.q: Why are the early years the foundation for later learning? Discuss the role of play and playful interactions in children's development.
questions.answer: Early childhood is a period of rapid development; quality care gives a safe, nurturing environment and decides how children learn and build relationships, while a poor start wastes human potential. Low ratios, small groups, sensitive trained caregivers and stimulating materials are needed. Play and playful interaction: from birth children explore through their senses; sensory play encourages discovery, independent thinking, imagination and creativity. It supports brain development (learning, memory), language (new words, songs), fine and gross motor skills (squeezing, pushing, throwing), cognitive growth (manipulating materials, new concepts), social interaction (sand and water play together) and body and space awareness.
